keep: The obituary that shamed him has never been found. The weapons works he bought in 1894 is in the record.
lede: The story goes that a French newspaper mistook his brother's death for his, called him the merchant of death, and that he wrote the prizes to clear his name. Nobody has ever produced the newspaper.
copy: Alfred Nobel was born in Stockholm on 21 October 1833, and his trade was making nitroglycerine safe enough to sell. In 1863 he patented a blasting cap to set it off. In 1864 an explosion at the family's works at Heleneborg killed five people, among them his younger brother Emil, who was twenty. Making nitroglycerine was banned inside the Stockholm city limits. In the spring of 1866 shipments of it blew up in transit and in storage. His answer, patented in Sweden in 1867, was to soak the oil into an earth called kieselguhr and sell it as dynamite. By his death he held 355 patents, with factories and laboratories in some 90 places in more than 20 countries.

Dynamite cut tunnels, but it was not the whole business. In 1887 he patented ballistite, a smokeless powder. The French state monopoly turned it down and Italy bought it, and a campaign in France accused him of industrial espionage. He left for San Remo in 1891. In 1894 he bought Bofors in western Sweden, with an iron mill and a weapons factory. A year earlier, on his sixtieth birthday, he had listed among his plans "patents for the soundless discharging of a gun" and "thinking about purchasing the Swedish mill Bofors". On 27 November 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, he signed his third and last will.

After bequests to family and to his executors, the rest of a fortune of about 33 million kronor was to be invested, and the interest paid each year as prizes to those who "have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind", in five equal parts. "No consideration" was to be given to nationality. Some of his relatives tried to break the will, with the support at first of King Oscar II, and Swedish conservatives called it unpatriotic, because the prizes ought to have gone to Swedes. The executors got the money through from 33 million to 31, and the settlement with the family capped any prize at three winners. He died at San Remo on 10 December 1896. The first prizes were given in 1901. His last instruction was that his arteries be severed after his death, and his body burned only once doctors had confirmed "clear signs of death".

bio.t: Nobel: The Enigmatic Alfred and His Prizes
bio.why: Recent, and built from archives in several countries. The year is the English edition's; the Swedish original came first. Read its account of 1888 before trusting the obituary story anywhere else.

contested: The obituary, the influence and two smaller things. Every telling of the obituary relies on the same two quotations, as Colin Schultz wrote in Smithsonian in 2013, and no copy of the article has been produced. The Foundation's own histories of his life, four of them opened for this entry, never mention it. Yet a member of its staff, Annika Pontikis, told Legacy.com that Nobel did see his obituary in advance. A short notice in Le Figaro of 15 April 1888, reporting a Mr Nobel dead at Cannes and corrected the next day, is said to exist; this house has the claim only from a Stack Exchange answer and has not seen the page. The second is Bertha von Suttner, the peace campaigner. The Foundation's chairman said in 1996 that his friendship with her was "probably" what mattered most to the peace prize; its earlier biographer, Nils Ringertz, wrote "no doubt". Neither cites a letter, and the often-quoted one about a machine of mass destruction has not been found in any Nobel source. Smaller: the Foundation's opening address of 1996 counts five dead at Heleneborg, where its other pages say several, and the date of 3 September 1864 is repeated widely but was not in anything opened here. The will's own English changed in 2018, when the Foundation replaced the old translation's "mankind" with "humankind"; the Norwegian Nobel Institute still prints the old one.
